bn_says: There are five Declensions in Latin, distinguished from each other by the final letter of the Stem
Pure Latin nouns of the First Declension regularly end, in the Nominative Singular, in -ă
Pure Latin nouns of the Second Declension end in -us, -er, -ir, Masculine; -um, Neuter
Nouns of the Third Declension end in -a, -e, -ī, -ō, -y, -c, -l, -n, -r, -s, -t, -x.
Nouns of the Fourth Declension end in -us Masculine, and -ū Neuter
Nouns of the Fifth Declension end in -ēs
In these the Masculine is declined like hortus, puer, or ager, the Feminine like porta, and the Neuter like bellum
Adjectives of three terminations in the Nominative Singular,—one for each gender
The Comparative is regularly formed by adding -ior (Neut. -ius) to the Stem of the Positive
the Superlative by adding -issimus (-a, -um) to the Stem of the Positive
